note: Splits fairness work by model scale and training paradigm, which matters when advising on fine tuning versus prompting.
title: A Survey on Fairness in Large Language Models
explain_beginner: Large language models learn from huge amounts of text written by people, and that text carries the biases and stereotypes present in society. This means the models can end up treating groups of people unfairly, for example by favoring certain genders or ethnicities in the responses they produce. This paper is a broad survey that pulls together the research on making these language models fairer. The authors point out that fixing bias looks different depending on the size and type of the model. For smaller, more customizable models, researchers can dig into the model's internal workings and retrain or adjust it directly. For today's largest models, which are mostly used through prompts rather than retrained from scratch, fixing bias mostly means clever prompt design or lightweight fine tuning after the fact. The survey catalogs many ways to measure bias and many ways to reduce it, but it also concludes that no single fix works reliably across every situation, and that current tools for detecting and measuring bias in the largest models are still immature and inconsistent with each other.
explain_business: For a business buying or deploying a large language model, this survey is a reminder that bias reduction is not a solved, one time fix, and no available metric fully certifies a model as fair. Vendors may report favorable scores on one fairness benchmark while the model still behaves unevenly across other measures or real use cases, because different fairness tests often do not agree with one another. Practically, companies should test any deployed model against their own use cases and demographic groups rather than trusting a single published benchmark score, and should expect that prompt based mitigations, such as adding fairness instructions to prompts, are the main lightweight tool for today's largest commercial models, though the paper notes such fixes are not always stable. There is a real cost implication too, since current best practice debiasing, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback, is expensive and resource intensive, so budgeting for ongoing fairness auditing, not a single upfront check, is the more realistic approach for any organization deploying these models at scale.
explain_practitioner: This is a survey rather than an original experiment, organizing prior work on fairness in large language models around a size based taxonomy: medium sized models, addressed through pre-training and fine-tuning, and today's largest models, addressed mainly through prompting since their internal representations are less accessible. For medium sized models it catalogs intrinsic bias metrics such as SEAT, CrowS-Pairs, and WinoBias, and extrinsic bias benchmarks such as BOLD and BBQ, alongside debiasing methods spanning pre-processing counterfactual data augmentation, in-processing disentanglement and contrastive learning, and post-processing embedding correction. For large models it reviews newer benchmarks like BiasAsker and FairPrism, and covers RLHF instruction tuning and prompt engineering as the dominant mitigations. The finding that matters most is the observation that intrinsic and extrinsic bias measures are not reliably correlated, so fairer internal representations do not guarantee fairer outputs, and different fairness metrics often disagree. A limitation the authors name directly is that benchmarks for large scale models remain neither diverse nor comprehensive enough, and low cost, reliable debiasing methods for large models are still lacking compared to resource heavy RLHF pipelines.
